sm: The host opens on the busiest travel week of the year, with about 80 million Americans traveling and roughly six million flying. He notes a Delta outage tied to its weight and balance system, coming just days after a similar United failure and a nationwide ground stop blamed on a replaced router in Arkansas. Delta and United use different, decades-old systems, and no one has explained why both failed so close together. He says 2026 is on pace for the highest cancellation rate since 2022.

He then walks through Department of Transportation figures for January to September. Alaska and Delta lead on on-time arrivals at about 78 percent, while Southwest and JetBlue each dropped about five points. JetBlue's cancellations more than tripled, Delta's nearly doubled, and American and its partners canceled the most flights overall. His advice is to avoid regional code share partners, which cancel far more often. He ends on the rise of private jets, which he calls nearly as dangerous per trip as motorcycles, and describes his own cramped, unnerving private flights.

The host contrasts today's flying with the era of supersonic jets and lavish first-class lounges. He says federal price regulation forced airlines to compete on quality, and tells the story of Southwest answering a Braniff fare cut with a choice between a matched fare or full price plus a bottle of liquor. Most customers took the liquor. He says Carter's 1978 deregulation changed everything, and plays a 1988 Saturday Night Live sketch about a filthy plane to show the results.

He notes that the left backed deregulation, citing Ted Kennedy, and quotes a Milken Institute article saying airline operating margins have averaged near zero since then, with many carriers lost and smaller airports losing flights. The article suggests letting foreign carriers fly domestic routes. He praises Emirates' premium economy seats and his own Qatar Airways flight to Kenya, which he calls the best of his life, and contrasts them with a bare Delta first-class seat.

He argues that unions and seniority-based layoffs during COVID hurt service and discouraged young people from aviation. He cites a study of thirty years of post-deregulation data showing higher fares in concentrated markets, worse service, and boom-and-bust profits with growing losses. He blames low margins and high turnover for poor service, and plays video of Spirit Airlines employees dumping a passenger's belongings in the trash. He concludes that zero profits mean airlines cannot pay for good employees.

The host says deregulation was not a mistake because people need cheap options, but the pendulum has swung so far that high-quality air travel exists only on private jets or foreign airlines. Coach has declined so much that first class, still 80 percent better, is objectively poor, and he calls TSA PreCheck a scam. He argues that progress is not automatic, that disorder naturally increases, and that leaders must maintain the conditions for improvement. He links the decline to demographic and political change. He says families now live far apart, so air travel is a necessity, and a system built on unreliable technology leaves people dependent and easier for leaders to control.
